chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl bin Ziyad and Ali bin Ibrahim, from his father, both together from Ibn Mahboub, from Ali bin Raib, from Abu Baseer who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who killed an insane man. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'If the insane man intended (to kill) him, so he defended himself, so he killed him, then there is nothing upon him from a retaliation (qawd), nor a wergild (diyah), and his inheritors would be given his wergild from the public treasury of the Muslims.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'And if he killed him from other than the insane happened to have intended (to kill) him, so there is no retaliation for the one from whom there is no retaliation. So I see the wergild to be upon his killer from his own wealth, to be handed over to the inheritors of the insane, and he should seek Forgiveness of Allah and repent to Him.'

key_terms.قَوَد: Retaliation (blood for blood) in Islamic jurisprudence

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling for killing an insane person in self-defense versus non-self-defense?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between intentional homicide and accidental killing of an insane person, ruling that in self-defense, the killer is exempt from both qisas (retaliation) and diyah (blood money), with compensation drawn from the public treasury (bayt al-mal). Conversely, if the killing was not in self-defense, the killer bears personal financial liability for the diyah and is encouraged to seek spiritual repentance, reflecting the Shia juristic principle that the insane lack full legal accountability (ahliyyah) for their actions.
